received.nothing: Nothing has been pushed at this service.
notLoaded: Shared Signals is not loaded in this process. The module registers no routes here, so there is nothing to report. Everything else on this console is unaffected.
off: SSF is turned off (ssf.enabled). The routes are still registered and answer 501 rather than 404, because the feature being off and the URL being wrong are different sentences to a client. The transmitter metadata still answers, so a receiver can discover that this service speaks SSF and is not currently doing it. Turn it back on in the settings at the foot of this page.
intro: The Shared Signals Framework (OpenID SSF 1.0, final 2 September 2025) is the one protocol family here that TALKS BACK. Every other family answers a request; this one delivers an event nobody asked for, at the moment it happens, to somebody who agreed in advance to be told. What it solves is that SAML and OpenID Connect authenticate at ONE INSTANT and the relying party then holds a session for hours whatever happens next.
pipe.before: SSF is the pipe and not the vocabulary. It defines how two parties agree a stream, who the events are about (RFC 9493), what they travel in (RFC 8417) and how they get there (RFC 8935 push, RFC 8936 poll) — and exactly TWO events of its own, both about the pipe. The vocabularies are CAEP (what happened to a session) and RISC (what happened to an account). CAEP is implemented — its eight session event types travel on the streams below, and
pipe.middle: carries the settings, the catalogue and the by-hand emit form while
pipe.after: counts what has been said about whom. RISC is the third part and is not here yet. What changed with CAEP is the sentence this page used to carry next: this service DOES now generate an event on its own, when a session starts, is presented or ends. caep.autoEmit puts the old behaviour back.
discovery.heading: Discovery
discovery.where: Everything a receiver needs is at {url}, which is never gated: a receiver has to be able to read what the endpoints are before it can authenticate to one. The issuer is {issuer} and every SET is signed with {alg}.
discovery.algorithm: That algorithm is ssf.signingAlgorithm and it reaches the whole table, post-quantum included — ML-DSA at three sizes, SLH-DSA at two, and the six composite ML-DSA + traditional ones — because a SET is signed through the same signer every other JWT here goes through. This is the document most worth signing that way: it records that something HAPPENED, RFC 8417 section 4.1.4 forbids it to expire, and it is therefore read long after it was written.
streams.heading: Streams
streams.none: No streams. A receiver creates one by POSTing a Stream Configuration to {endpoint}. There is deliberately no “create a stream” form here: a stream carries a delivery endpoint THIS SERVICE WILL DIAL, and the one place that URL may come from is a receiver that authenticated and asked — see ssf/ssf_http.ts.
pushed.heading: Pushed at this service
pushed.note: The roles reversed. POST /ssf/receive accepts a Security Event Token pushed AT this service, which is what a client acting as the TRANSMITTER sends to. It accepts one whose signature does not verify and reports why — a receiver that refused could not show anybody what arrived, which is the question being asked. ssf.receiveRequireSignature turns the 400 on.
